title: The Serpent's Coil
story:
In a deep pool of the Yamuna lived Kaliya, a king of serpents whose poison had made the river deadly and driven the cowherds of Vrindavan from its banks. Krishna, a boy of the village, had gone down into that water to drive the serpent out, and there, in the deep, the serpent had him.

Kaliya struck without warning. He bit the boy in the yellow cloth who stood playing in the water without a trace of fear, and then he wound his coils about him, round and round, holding him fast. In the dark of the pool Krishna lay wrapped in the serpent's body, and he did not move.

On the bank the cowherd boys had seen it. Their friend, whom they loved more than their own lives, lay bound and still in the water, and the sight undid them. Grief and terror and sorrow came over them all at once, their minds gave way, and they dropped where they stood. The cows and the bulls and the young calves lowed and cried out in their own tongue, until it sounded like the whole pasture mourning at once.

Far off in Vrindavan, terrible omens began to appear, three kinds of them, one after another, the sort that make men certain death has come. The cowherds saw them and were stricken with fear. Led by Nanda, Krishna's father, with the children and the old men and the women, everyone down to the last — for they all lived by Krishna the way cattle live by grass — they poured out of the village to search for him. Balarama, Krishna's elder brother, went with them, watching over the frightened crowd.

They followed the marks his feet had left in the dust, footprints stamped with the sign of a lotus, a barley grain, a goad, a thunderbolt and a banner. The trail led them straight to the water. There, in the depths of the pool, they found him: Krishna, wrapped in the serpent's coils, not moving, while around the shore his bewildered friends and the lowing cattle stood in a ring. What they saw fell on them like the end of everything, and it crushed them.

The gopis, whose hearts lived in him, stood remembering his friendship, his smile, the way he looked at them, the things he said — and all the world seemed empty to them, as if the sun had gone out of every sky at once. They gathered around his mother Yashoda, who had come running after her child, held her up, and wept with her. Over and over they told the old, beloved stories of Vrindavan, their eyes fixed on Krishna's face in the water, until they looked like people who had already died of grief.

And still he did not move. The water lay dark and heavy, and the serpent's coils held.
reflection: The verses spend little time on the serpent and much on what his grip costs everyone else — the fallen boys, the lowing cattle, the omens, the mother held up by the gopis, the world gone empty. Peril here is measured in the grief of those who watch, which is what makes the stillness of the water so unbearable.
content_note: A serpent's venomous grip on Krishna is described briefly; the grief of his family and friends is vivid but restrained.
next_story_tease: But the serpent's grip was about to become a stage — Krishna would rise and dance upon those hoods.
hero_scene: Kaliya's coils wrapped around the motionless Krishna in the dark water, while on the bank the cowherds, gopis, Nanda and Yashoda stand weeping, the cattle lowing, the pool churned and smoking.
